posts.title: The Capitalist Contradiction
posts.content:
Modernist styles then become stamped with bureaucratic connotation, so that to break with it radically produces some feeling of ‘relief,’ even though what replaces it is neither Utopia nor democracy, but simply the private-corporate constructions of the post-welfare-state postmodern” (Jameson, 1991, p. 270). I watch that bait-and-switch play out every day: we swap yesterday’s concrete welfare-state blocks for glass atria, neon lounges, and gamified dashboards, sigh with relief, and never notice the same old command grid still humming. Walls funnel us, cameras track us—the paint job changed, not the power. Jameson calls this sleight of hand “overdetermination in ambivalence,” where the very same form scans as plebeian and bureaucratic at once, leaving us too dizzy to decide whether to cheer or revolt (p. 270).

Late-capitalist America treats social roles the way fast fashion treats clothing lines: grab the label, flaunt it, discard it when the algorithm demands something new. Everyone wants to be a creative director, data scientist, or activist—not because they have mastered the craft, but because the title itself carries a prestigious aura. When history is flattened into “what sells, what circulates—[and] starts to look like the ultimate unquestionable reality” (Jameson, 1991, pp. 279-280), the depth of a vocation evaporates; identity turns into a pop-up shop. School primed us for that swap. From the Prussian bell schedule to the college résumé factory, we learned to chase external cues, brand ourselves for the next niche, and call obedience “leadership.” Marx would call it alienation: our capacity for genuine creation gets rented out to whichever industry is paying.

That same market logic can also undermine historical trauma and political struggle. Late capitalism strips raw memory—women’s suffrage, Stonewall, Black liberation—of moral weight and re-issues it as consumable style: ready-meal kits instead of paid housework, rainbow cereal each June instead of queer healthcare, #BLM hoodies silk-screened in sweatshops. Movements like feminism, BLM, and LGBTQ+ pride become both lucrative niches and real sites of resistance, their imagery sold at festival booths even as the organizing beneath it still wrestles for concessions the system never volunteers. Miss one side and you miss the dialectic; hold both and the deeper irony snaps into focus: a society that chants “be an individual” while engineering ever-finer templates for us to buy, wear, and shred on command.

School is where the contradiction first burrows under our skin. The bell-and-row routine—marketed as equal access to knowledge—taught us to shelve curiosity, change tasks on cue, and accept discomfort as usual. Now, the chalkboard is a 3D-printer lab, and the hall pass is a QR code, but the reflex endures: hear the ping, pivot; hit the rubric, crank out the deliverable. By graduation, we brand ourselves “innovators” while fine-tuning the machinery that confines us, mistaking compliance for creativity. Unless we call out this ambivalence—locker bell to key-card ping, protest tee to premium streetwear—we will continue to applaud stylish upgrades as a form of freedom. At the same time, the deeper hierarchy remains firmly in place beneath the surface.

posts.title: Player One
posts.content:
There is this weird omnipresence in my life, where I was practically expected to know how to play a video game in everyday life. I was no more than 5 years old when I was handed a controller for my dad’s original Xbox. There is a sentiment and more nuanced meaning behind that, but we will get there. Regarding a controller, at 5 years old, I was expected to have “control” over something outside of myself, and I barely had much to begin with. When a sudden loss of control becomes overwhelming, these moments paralyse my body. Even though someone can hand me a controller at any moment, and I can use it better than the majority, you take me back to when I wasn't always looked at to maintain some semblance of “control,” I will turn to no more than Medusa's example.

High expectations have always been something I have been worried about. Only until I was getting bullied and my grades dropped did they ever think to ask if I was okay. It was only inconvenient to them as their way of determining whether I was a good kid was a grade report on what I retained or used daily. Passing a test is one thing, but using the applicable skills in school in daily life is a different perspective I take on school. If you have access to information and choose not to learn, such is doing a disservice to those who provide that information; then again, gatekeeping can occur, a topic for another day, but it still stands where it is.
        That same controller is on my mind. That same week, my parents expected me to be an adult. I was left home alone for the first and not the last time, which made me a little hesitant and worried. Afterwards, I made a snack, did homework, and watched TV. My parents felt terrible, yet I wasn't sure what they did that was wrong, as if I was the one thrown off by their reaction.

There has always been an emphasis on light in my life; even in the darkest moments, there was something to intrigue me, simple but always appreciative. When I was younger, my grandparent's front door entrance had a beautiful glass-style door, and when light rays in the morning shone through that glass, the rays would cast rainbows on the old, tattered, but still somewhat luxurious rug. It is a kind of rug with many designs and a sense of weight. These rays traced upon this rug in a way that danced in my mind even so young. Still, to this day, I can recount the contentment and appreciation for such an observation. The warmth of the sun's rays and the texture of that new but old rug are simple pleasures. I miss being so far away from such simple moments.

posts.title: In the Shadow of Loss
posts.content:
Honestly, it's been a journey through not just one or two but numerous deaths within a short span of a year and a half. While I understand that death is inevitable as we grow older, nothing could have prepared me for this. As it all began to unfold, the grieving process for one loved one was quickly overshadowed by another loss, making the already unforgiving process even more difficult. Creating this piece allowed me to honestly confront what death means to me and explore my relationship with it. Experiencing one death is hard enough, but enduring multiple losses in such a brief period diminishes one's ability to cope with the turmoil that comes from losing these relationships.

This exploration of death and grief through my art led to moments of profound connection, like when I found myself in the photo studio, speaking with my significant other’s father—who, as you might have noticed, is represented by the golden prayer hands in the image. It’s fascinating to see how we imbue inanimate objects with human qualities and how deeply they resonate with us when they become tied to memories of those we’ve lost.

As I continued to delve into this deeply personal project, navigating my relationship with death, I never anticipated that I would experience yet another loss while still creating it.

It was a day like any other. I woke up with plans to meet a friend for coffee, where we’d talk about his involvement in this project. There’s something strange about death—it catches you off guard, even when you’re not expecting it, and leaves you with an unsettling sense of powerlessness. Mid-conversation at the coffee shop, I got a call. “Hell—” I barely began to say before I was interrupted: “Great Grandma passed in her sleep last night.” When I heard those words, it was as if a looming shadow appeared behind me, placing a heavy weight in my hands. Without hesitation, I took it, quietly sitting with the burden while the shadow seemed to linger, waiting for my reaction—whether I’d break down or set it aside, as I had with the other losses in my life.

As the wheels of my car slowly roll into the funeral home's parking lot, gravel crunching audibly heard and felt through the pedals, I turn behind as if someone said my name. That same tall looming shadow is sitting there; he taps me and hands me that weight, and this foreboding silence occurs in my voice as if there was nothing right I could say despite my great-grandmother's death.

Acceptance is perhaps the most daunting challenge when facing death—coming to terms with the stark reality that it is beyond our control. As I entered the funeral home, a profound sense of melancholy enveloped me. I found myself seated before the coffin, hesitating to look inside. When I finally did, I saw her lying there, devoid of life. The vibrant humor, the lively spark that once animated her, was now absent, replaced by an overwhelming weight that seemed to pin me in place, immobilizing me with its heaviness.

Amid this suffocating grief, I felt an urgent need to break away, to find a way to process the torrent of emotions coursing through me. Instinctively, I reached for my camera and began to walk. There was no specific direction, no clear subject in mind—just a compulsion to capture something that might help me contain and make sense of my emotions. It was as if I was trying to distill the chaos within me into the frame of a photograph, using the lens to record and preserve the rawness of what I was feeling and seeing.

My wandering led me across the street from the funeral home, where I stood before a church. I started to take pictures drawn to the symbolism of the setting. Nearby, street signs caught my attention, each marked "One Way," pointing in contradictory directions. The irony was striking—death is the ultimate one-way journey, a path from which no return exists. The juxtaposition of these signs with the solemnity of the moment resonated deeply with me, reflecting the inescapable finality of the loss I was grappling with.
